# Plan: rate limiting for the orders API

One customer's script created 40,000 orders in ten minutes last week and slowed every other customer down. I want to add rate limiting to `src/server.ts` and ship it this week.

What we have:

- 3 instances of `src/server.ts` behind a round-robin load balancer.
- A Redis 7 cluster already used for sessions by another service; we may use it.
- `POST /orders` writes to Postgres and is the expensive call; `GET /orders` is cheap.
- About 20 enterprise customers have scripted integrations that legitimately burst.

Not decided yet:

- What to key the limit on: `x-customer-id`, client IP, or both.
- Algorithm: fixed window, sliding window, or token bucket.
- Where counters live: Redis, or in each instance's memory.
- What happens if the counter store is unreachable: let requests through or reject them.
- How enterprise customers get higher limits, and who owns those numbers.
- What a rejected client sees.
- How to roll it out without breaking the enterprise integrations.

content.name: ask

evidence.note: Header read directly off the request, no signature/token check anywhere in the repo

brief.how: If upstream verifies or mints the header (API gateway, signed token), keying purely on it is safe and I defer keying to round 2 with that assumption. If it's raw client-supplied, any scripted client can forge another customer's id and burn their quota, so authentication must be decided before keying.
risks: Unverified identity + per-customer quotas = trivial quota-striking attack
If you answer 'it's verified upstream' and it isn't, the limiter inherits that hole
brief.what: Whether the `x-customer-id` header is trustworthy as a rate-limit key. In this repo nothing checks it: no signature, no token, no lookup table. The plan keys limits on identity, but a spoofable key means one abusive client can exhaust another customer's limit, which is worse than no limiter.
brief.where: `src/server.ts:8` reads `x-customer-id` off the incoming request and trusts it; `src/orders.ts` uses it bare for Postgres writes.

options.description: LB/API gateway mints or validates the id; the limiter may trust it
options.holds_when: There is auth middleware or a gateway in front of the 3 instances that stamps this header itself
options.label: Verified upstream
options.tradeoff: Safe to key on the id; no new auth code needed in the limiter

options.description: Header is client-supplied; anything with it is accepted
options.holds_when: Requests could hit server.ts directly, bypassing the LB
options.label: Not verified, client-supplied
options.tradeoff: Ship with the hole and fix auth later

options.description: Requests could hit server.ts directly; add a signed-id or key check as part of this work
options.holds_when: Customers are 20 known enterprises; issuing a static key per customer is a one-week effort
options.label: Not verified — verify as part of this plan
options.tradeoff: Slightly grows the plan, but removes an attack that defeats the limiter itself

options.description: IP trust or signed-header trust; ask me a follow-up
options.holds_when: No single answer covers what exists
options.label: It's more complicated — I'll describe
options.tradeoff: Round 2 depends on your description

questions.question: Is `x-customer-id` verified by anything upstream of `src/server.ts` (API gateway, load balancer that mints it, signed token), or is it whatever the client sends?

evidence.note: 3 instances make single-instance counters wrong by construction

brief.how: Redis makes the limit mean the same thing for every request and survives restarts; cost is a new runtime dependency on the rate-limit hot path. In-memory is zero-dependency but the limit silently becomes 'per instance', and count values then need dividing by 3 — a trap six months from now.
risks: Shared-cluster contention: rate-limit Lua calls mix with session traffic; a slow key or a failover blocks the hot path
Latency: every POST gains a Redis round-trip that grows with algorithm strictness
brief.what: Whether the counters live in Redis or in each instance's memory. With 3 instances behind a round-robin LB (PLAN.md:7), an in-memory counter is per instance: a client at 10 req/s sees 30 effective req/s, and the limit is enforced only 1/3 of the time. The plan lists this as open; the deployment fact makes the alternatives unequal.
brief.where: 3 instances of `src/server.ts` behind a round-robin LB; Redis 7 cluster already shared with a sessions service (PLAN.md:6-8).

options.description: Dedicated key namespace, e.g. `rl:`, on the shared cluster; document blast radius and set capacity headroom
options.holds_when: The cluster has headroom and a failover here shouldn't take sessions down
options.label: Redis, separate namespace
options.tradeoff: Correct global counts; borrows infra reliability from another service

options.description: Free capacity and failure isolation; this week's rollout grows a provisioning step
options.holds_when: You can pitch a small new Redis without a procurement fight
options.label: New small Redis instance just for rate limits
options.tradeoff: Isolation, at the cost of one more runtime to operate

options.description: Accept effective limit ≈ 3× configured and inconsistent enforcement
options.holds_when: You plan TTLs-friendly rough limiting only, and 3× drift is fine
options.label: In-memory on each instance
options.tradeoff: Zero new infra, correct enforcement sacrificed

questions.question: Where do the counters live — Redis shared with sessions, or in each instance's memory?

evidence.note: Bursty legitimate traffic rules out a plain fixed window

brief.how: Token bucket justifies its extra state: one bucket per customer, configured with a burst size and a refill rate, so pacing is the customer's choice — exactly what enterprise scripts want. Fixed/sliding windows punish a burst for the whole window/reject harmless mid-window bursts. All three work in Redis (via Lua) or in memory, so this doesn't wait for Q2.
risks: Two numbers per tier (burst + rate) instead of one — tier owner has to reason about both
brief.what: Which rate-limiting algorithm. The deciding constraint is in the plan: ~20 enterprise customers legitimately burst (PLAN.md:10). A fixed window allows 2× bursts at window boundaries and rejects mid-window bursts that would be harmless on average; a sliding window counter smooths that; a token bucket makes burst a first-class, customer-visible knob.
brief.where: Algorithm is undecided (PLAN.md:15); the traffic fact is 'enterprise customers with scripted integrations that legitimately burst'.

options.description: Customer burns tokens in bursts, refills at the steady rate; burst size is a tier parameter
options.holds_when: Scripts poll hourly and do 200 requests in one go
options.label: Token bucket
options.tradeoff: Burst-native tuning; needs an atomic check-and-decrement in Redis (Lua)

options.description: Counts previous window weighted by its remainder; smooths the 2× boundary burst
options.holds_when: You want the cheapest correct thing and one number per tier
options.label: Sliding window counter
options.tradeoff: One number per tier; app logic slightly fancier than fixed window

options.description: One number per tier, ~15 lines of stateless code, more tolerant of edge bursts
options.holds_when: You want this done in one day and are fine with the worst-case burst shape
options.label: Fixed window
options.tradeoff: Cheapest; bursts at boundaries get through at 2× the limit

options.description: Very tight, stateless per check, opaque math to maintain
options.holds_when: You expect abusers to probe the boundaries
options.label: GCRA / leaky bucket
options.tradeoff: Tightest enforcement, hardest to explain to customers

evidence.note: Response shape for rejected clients is an open bullet

brief.how: Retry-After is needed for script correctness: with token bucket or sliding window you can compute when a retry should succeed, so scripts back off for one line instead of spin-polling. Limit headers (RateLimit-*/X-RateLimit-*) let customer engineers pre-empt the 429 rather than debug one after it lands.
risks: Machine-readable JSON means a schema the 20 integrations may codify against — keep it flat and immutable
brief.what: What a rejected client gets. This decides not just a status code but what the 20 customer engineering teams have to parse and honor, and what their dashboards show when they hit the wall. The plan leaves it undecided (PLAN.md:19).
brief.where: PLAN.md:19 lists 'What a rejected client sees' as undecided; there is currently no rejection path for limits, only the 401 for a missing header at src/server.ts:8.

options.description: 429 status, JSON {error: 'rate_limited', retryAfterSeconds}, Retry-After header, and X-RateLimit-Limit/Remaining/Reset on both 429 and 200 responses
options.holds_when: Integrations are real code that other engineers will read in six months
options.label: 429 + Retry-After + limit headers + JSON body
options.tradeoff: Best client ergonomics, most code

options.description: 429 + JSON body, no headers; clients back off on their own
options.holds_when: You don't want header plumbing on this path
options.label: 429 + JSON body, no limit headers
options.tradeoff: Machinable, half complete

options.description: 429 and a plain-text message; no contract, integrations guess
options.holds_when: You're launching by end of week and treating integrations as break-glass
options.label: 429 only, no body
options.tradeoff: Cheapest, worst for the 20 customers debugging it

questions.question: What does a rejected request return?

evidence.note: Both questions stacked in one plan bullet: storage AND ownership

brief.how: A config file is reviewable and versioned with deploy; a database table allows change without redeploy but adds a read path and a mutation surface you'd have to build. With ~20 customers and no self-serve portal, config wins. Who signs off on the numbers is a separate round-2 question that hangs off this storage answer.
risks: Config-file overrides tempt a scaled change at 2am in prod — name who edits and how it lands
brief.what: Where enterprise tier limits live, now that tier changes are a named need (PLAN.md:18). Who owns the numbers is a policy question; storage is a mechanism question and can be decided independently.
brief.where: How customers get higher limits is undecided (PLAN.md:18); ~20 known enterprise customers

options.description: e.g. limits.json checked into the repo with the default and per-customer overrides
options.holds_when: Number changes are rare and code review is acceptable for them
options.label: Static config file
options.tradeoff: Boring and reviewable; edits need a deploy

options.description: Rows keyed by customer id, loaded on boot or polled
options.holds_when: Sales or CS occasionally adjusts a tier without an engineer
options.label: Database table
options.tradeoff: Edits without deploy; new code path to load and cache

options.description: Same file/table but with a comment header naming the owner per tier
options.holds_when: You want enforcement built before deciding ownership
options.label: Decide storage now, ownership later
options.tradeoff: Keeps this week's scope; leaves a named gap in the plan

questions.question: Where are the per-customer limits stored?

evidence.note: Plan itself says only POST is expensive
Both verbs share the same handler and the same x-customer-id branch

brief.how: Enforcing on POST only matches the failure observed and keeps the cheap path free; the bucket-on-customer design still lets you extend to GET later without reworking keys or tiers. Deciding now also decides whether the ship-date is gated on GET discussions with 20 customers.
risks: A runaway integration of GET reads and Postgres selects can still load the DB — confirm the read path is actually cheap at 40k/s
brief.what: Whether GET /orders is included. PLAN.md:9 says POST is the expensive call and GET is cheap, but the limiter nominally sits in front of both; enforcing only POST is a scope decision the plan doesn't make for you.
brief.where: Both verbs hit the same handler path (src/server.ts:10-16) and the same `x-customer-id` branch.

options.description: The one observed to melt things; ship with the tight blast radius
options.holds_when: GET really is just a Postgres select on this customer's rows
options.label: POST /orders only
options.tradeoff: Smallest scope; leaves the plan open if GET-traffic abuse shows up later

options.description: Same key, separate counters per verb
options.holds_when: You want the limiter to count work that's actually different but still protect the API
options.label: POST and GET /orders, separate buckets
options.tradeoff: Covers read abuse too, at the cost of twice the state

options.description: Count every route on one shared per-customer bucket, making the tier a single number across the API
options.holds_when: The customer writes and reads about equally in a burst
options.label: POST and GET /orders, shared bucket
options.tradeoff: One number per customer, but reads crowd out writes

options.description: One shared bucket across all routes on the service, treating the whole thing as one resource
options.label: All routes including 404s and auth failures
options.tradeoff: Uniform, over-limit applies to paths you hadn't planned to defend

evidence.note: 3 instances make single-instance counters wrong by construction

brief.how: Redis makes the limit mean the same thing for every request and survives restarts; cost is a new runtime dependency on the rate-limit hot path. In-memory is zero-dependency but the limit silently becomes 'per instance', and count values then need dividing by 3 — a trap six months from now.
risks: Shared-cluster contention: rate-limit Lua calls mix with session traffic; a slow key or a failover blocks the hot path
Latency: every POST gains a Redis round-trip that grows with algorithm strictness
brief.what: Whether the counters live in Redis or in each instance's memory. With 3 instances behind a round-robin LB (PLAN.md:7), an in-memory counter is per instance: a client at 10 req/s sees 30 effective req/s, and the limit is enforced only 1/3 of the time. The plan lists this as open; the deployment fact makes the alternatives unequal.
brief.where: 3 instances of `src/server.ts` behind a round-robin LB; Redis 7 cluster already shared with a sessions service (PLAN.md:6-8).

evidence.note: Bursty legitimate traffic rules out a plain fixed window

brief.how: Token bucket justifies its extra state: one bucket per customer, configured with a burst size and a refill rate, so pacing is the customer's choice — exactly what enterprise scripts want. Fixed/sliding windows punish a burst for the whole window/reject harmless mid-window bursts. All three work in Redis (via Lua) or in memory, so this doesn't wait for Q2.
risks: Two numbers per tier (burst + rate) instead of one — tier owner has to reason about both
brief.what: Which rate-limiting algorithm. The deciding constraint is in the plan: ~20 enterprise customers legitimately burst (PLAN.md:10). A fixed window allows 2× bursts at window boundaries and rejects mid-window bursts that would be harmless on average; a sliding window counter smooths that; a token bucket makes burst a first-class, customer-visible knob.
brief.where: Algorithm is undecided (PLAN.md:15); the traffic fact is 'enterprise customers with scripted integrations that legitimately burst'.
